name: Hair dye / bleaching

lead: Hair dye and bleach change hair color on the spot: lighter, darker, or gray covered. In style circles they are used to change contrast with the skin and eyes and give a visibly new look. Reports say 50 to 80 percent of women in the US, Europe and Japan have used hair dye.

Permanent dye and bleach use an oxidizer and an alkaline agent such as ammonia to open the hair cuticle; bleach oxidizes melanin to lighten, while dye deposits color. Lower-strength dyes coat or lightly penetrate the hair without lightening. The techniques are well established, though no studies test whether coloring improves attractiveness.

paras: People color at a salon or at home, with bleach followed by toner for lighter shades and a permanent or semi-permanent dye for darker or natural-looking color. Roots need touching up as hair grows, and bleached hair is usually given extra conditioning.

Reported risks are skin irritation, PPD allergy, hair breakage, skin staining and unexpected color. Studies linking dye to cancer are limited and inconsistent, and the EU restricts about 45 hair dye chemicals.

chain: Different contrast with skin and eyes
angle.text: Bleaching hair lighter or dyeing it darker changes your contrast with your skin and eyes and covers gray, and the new color is visible immediately. Hair coloring is a well-established cosmetic method used by a large share of adults.

lead: Hair coloring changes the color of head hair, typically to cover gray, change a look or restore color after bleaching or sun exposure. In looksmaxxing and style discussions it is raised as a way to alter contrast, for example bleaching hair lighter or dyeing it darker. Reports say 50 to 80 percent of women in the US, Europe and Japan have used hair dye.[1]

Bleaching lightens hair by oxidizing melanin, using hydrogen peroxide with an alkaline agent such as ammonia.[1] Documented risks include skin irritation, allergy, hair breakage and unexpected color. Studies on hair dye and cancer risk are described as limited and inconsistent.[1]
infobox: Permanent, demi-permanent, semi-permanent, temporary dyes; bleaching
About 6% peroxide at home, up to 12% in salons[1]

paras: Permanent dye uses ammonia and an oxidizing developer to open the hair cuticle and deposit color in the cortex. Demi-permanent dye uses a lower peroxide level and cannot lighten hair, and semi-permanent dye, which can still contain PPD, lasts about 4 to 8 shampoos. Temporary products wash out in one shampoo.[1]
Vivid or fashion colors contain tint but no developer, so on dark hair they usually require bleaching first.[1]
Bleaching breaks down melanin by oxidation, releasing oxygen gas. Bleached hair can turn brassy or yellow, and toners and purple shampoos are used to correct undertones.[1]

Hair dye recipes appear in Assyrian herbals from about 2177 BCE, and the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) describes dyeing gray hair. Diodorus Siculus described Celtic peoples bleaching hair with lime.[1] Perkin's discovery of mauveine in 1856 launched synthetic dyes, Eugene Schueller is credited with the first synthetic hair dye in 1907, and Schwarzkopf launched a home color product in 1947.[1]

Dye can cause skin irritation, allergic reactions, hair breakage and skin staining. PPD-based dyes have been controversial, symptoms can appear hours to a day later, and manufacturers recommend patch testing, which some European dermatologists advise against for self-testing.[1]

The IARC has reported that some hair dyes and ingredients can be considered mutagenic or carcinogenic. Studies have associated hair dye with certain cancers, and a 2017 meta-analysis suggested roughly 20 percent higher breast cancer risk among users, but evidence overall is described as limited and inconsistent.[1] The EU restricts about 45 chemicals in hair dyes.[1]

No studies found testing hair color change as a means of improving attractiveness. Epidemiological studies on hair dye use and health include the Copenhagen City Heart Study (2016, 7,684 women followed for 37 years) and a 2018 meta-analysis on breast cancer risk.[1]
